synopsis: Standards bodies run committees, hold votes and publish standards; ISO and IEC provide an international baseline, while EN texts can carry legal weight in Europe through the harmonization process [f15016, f15031, f15077]. For heavy off-road validation, program-level collision-mitigation acceptance values should not be described as ISO mandates without a normative clause, and national adoptions may differ from their originals [f2636, f15032]. The booklet reports no standards-body or industry-group study establishing whether on-road simulation methods transfer to off-road machines; ASAM's 2023 off-road workshop led to a concept project, but its evidence is expert opinion rather than normative evidence, and standardized simulation-quality metrics remain absent [f1248, f7191, f7197, f15024]. European adoption of ISO 19014-1 was in CEN approval alongside the 2026 series changes, while the glossary's assertion that Standards Australia publishes AS 21815.1:2023 sits in tension with Chapter 3's failure to locate its catalogue entry [f2211, f15179, f15027, f2873]. Aviation offers an acceptance precedent through standards bodies and authorities, with DO-385 and ED-256 published in October 2018, but confidence in credibility frameworks remains contested by a 2026 preprint calling them “largely declarative” [f1470, f15747, f10324].
